answer:
A 2026 trial in Clinical Nutrition found that time-restricted eating was not more beneficial for reducing body weight than daily calorie restriction [2]. The calorie-restriction-only group lost 6.3 kg, and the 1.8 kg difference was not statistically significant [2]. In that trial, intermittent fasting and continuous calorie restriction produced comparable weight loss when calories were matched [2].

An earlier 2025 trial in Annals of Internal Medicine found that 4:3 intermittent fasting outperformed daily caloric restriction by 2.89 kg, a statistically significant difference [3]. After 12 months, the fasting group lost 7.6% of body weight, compared with 5.0% in the daily-restriction group [3][4]. More than half (58%) of fasting participants achieved at least 5% weight loss, versus 47% on daily restriction [3][4]. Harvard Health also reported the 4:3 group lost about 6 more pounds than the calorie-restriction group after one year [1].

So the answer depends on the trial: one recent study shows a modest advantage for 4:3 fasting, while the most recent trial shows comparable weight loss [2][3].
